questions.text: Explain self-attention. Why Q, K and V?
points: Each token emits three projections: query (what I'm looking for), key (what I offer), value (what I pass on)
Scores = Q·Kᵀ, scaled by √d_k (stops softmax saturating), masked, softmaxed → weighted sum of V
Every position attends to every other in one step — that's the win over recurrence
Multi-head = several subspaces in parallel: syntax, coreference, position
Cost is O(n²) in sequence length — the root of every long-context problem
questions.badge: Evergreen
questions.flow: project QKV → scaled dot product → mask → softmax → weight V → heads in parallel
questions.trap: describing it as "the model focuses on important words" — that's the metaphor, not the mechanism

drill.prompt: from jbtiq_dl Q12: "Explain Q, K, V to me like I'm a strong backend engineer who has never seen attention."
drill.hint: Split prefill from decode. Which phase is compute-bound, which is memory-bandwidth-bound, and what does the KV cache convert between?
points: Mechanics in one breath: each token's Q dots against all Ks, softmax weights the Vs — attention is each position querying the whole past. Cost over a sequence of length n is O(n²) in compute and the KV tensors grow O(n) per layer per head.

Prefill (the prompt pass) does the full n² attention in parallel — compute-bound, sets time-to-first-token. Decode generates one token at a time, each reading the entire KV cache — memory-bandwidth-bound, sets time-per-output-token. Two different bottlenecks, two different optimizations.

The KV cache trades recompute for memory: without it every new token re-encodes the whole prefix; with it, decode is O(n) reads per token but the cache itself becomes the scarce resource — cache size scales with layers × heads × context × batch, and it's what limits concurrent sequences on a GPU.

This split explains the serving toolbox: batching helps decode (amortize weight reads), GQA/MQA shrink the KV cache, FlashAttention reduces memory traffic in prefill, and long contexts hurt both phases in different ways.
Say the architect's summary: LLM serving economics is mostly memory bandwidth and KV-cache real estate, not FLOPs.
drill.oneLiner: Prefill is quadratic and compute-bound, decode is linear per token but memory-bandwidth-bound reading the KV cache — and since the cache scales with context times batch, serving economics is really a KV-cache real-estate problem.

questions.text: Why did decoder-only win?
points: One objective — next-token prediction — scales on raw unlabelled text with no task design
Every task becomes generation: classification, extraction, translation, all one interface
Encoder-decoder still wins where input/output are genuinely distinct and fixed (translation, some seq2seq)
Encoder-only (BERT) remains right for embeddings and classification — that's your retriever
The win was scaling simplicity, not architectural superiority
questions.badge: Evergreen
questions.flow: one self-supervised objective → scales on any text → every task is generation
questions.trap: claiming decoder-only is strictly better — your embedding model is encoder-only

drill.prompt: from jbtiq_dl Q20: "Encoder-only, decoder-only, encoder-decoder — one exemplar each, and when is each family the right call?"
drill.hint: Think about the training signal per token, task generality, and what caching needs at inference.
points: Training efficiency: next-token prediction gives a loss signal at every position of every sequence, on raw text at web scale — no task-specific heads, no span-corruption design choices. Simplicity scaled.

Task universality: everything — translation, QA, classification, dialogue — reduces to continue this text; in-context learning fell out of that framing, and one model serves all tasks without architectural surgery.

Inference mechanics: causal attention makes the KV cache trivially incremental — each new token attends to a fixed, append-only past. Encoder-decoder buys bidirectional understanding at the cost of a two-stack pipeline that's harder to serve and doesn't stream as naturally.

Nuance to say: encoders aren't dead — embedding and reranking models are encoder-style because bidirectional context is exactly right for representation, not generation. The victory is per-role, not absolute.
drill.oneLiner: Next-token prediction gives dense supervision on raw text, every task reduces to continuation, and causal attention makes KV caching trivial — decoder-only won generation while encoders kept the representation jobs.

questions.text: What's in the KV cache, and why does it dominate memory?
points: Caches K and V per token, per layer, per head so each new token isn't recomputed
Turns per-token generation from O(n²) recompute into O(n) — without it decoding is unusable
Size ≈ 2 × layers × heads × head_dim × seq_len × batch × dtype — grows linearly with context and batch
It, not weights, is what caps your concurrency at long context
Mitigations: GQA/MQA (fewer KV heads), quantised cache, paged attention, offload/eviction
questions.badge: Trending — recurs on Devinterview LLM repos + inference-optimization blogs (NVIDIA-class) + LLM-infra JDs (2025–26)
questions.flow: cache K,V per layer → linear growth with context × batch → GQA + paging to survive it
questions.trap: saying "it caches the prompt" — it's per-layer tensors, and it's your real memory budget

drill.prompt: from jbtiq_dl Q18: "Your chat product's per-token compute is fine, but memory per concurrent conversation is blowing up. What is the KV cache, and why is it the thing that hurts?"
drill.badge: Trending — recurs on Devinterview LLM repos + inference-optimization blogs (NVIDIA-class) + LLM-infra JDs (2025–26)
drill.hint: What would each decode step have to recompute without it? Then write the size formula in your head and read off which factors grow.
points: Each decode step attends over all previous tokens' K and V. Recomputing them every step is O(n²) per token; caching K,V per layer per head makes each new token O(n) — the cache is what makes autoregressive serving viable.
Size ≈ 2 × layers × kv_heads × head_dim × seq_len × bytes × batch — linear in context length and in concurrent users. At long context it rivals or exceeds the weights themselves.
Consequence: decode becomes memory-bandwidth-bound — the cache must be re-read every step — so long context is a memory problem, not a compute problem.
Mitigations ladder (each is its own question): GQA/MQA (fewer kv_heads, Q21), KV quantization (fewer bytes), PagedAttention (no fragmentation, Q37), sliding-window attention (bounded seq_len, Q23).
drill.oneLiner: The KV cache trades memory for compute — O(n) decode instead of O(n²) — and its size grows linearly with context times concurrency, which is exactly why serving memory, not FLOPs, is the binding constraint.
drill.followUp: "So what's the first lever you'd pull?" → GQA is baked in at pretraining; at serving time, paging + KV quantization.

questions.text: How does the model know token order? Why RoPE?
points: Attention is permutation-invariant — position must be injected or it's a bag of words
Learned absolute embeddings don't extrapolate past training length
RoPE rotates Q and K by position, so the dot product depends on relative distance
That relative property is what makes context extension possible — NTK/YaRN scaling stretch the rotation
ALiBi takes a different route: a distance penalty on scores
questions.badge: Evergreen
questions.flow: attention has no order → inject position → RoPE makes it relative → rotation can be scaled to extend
questions.trap: not connecting RoPE to why long-context extension works at all

drill.prompt: from jbtiq_dl Q15: "Attention is permutation-invariant. What are your options for injecting order, and what does modern practice actually use?"
drill.hint: Four families: two absolute, two relative. Which one survives in current decoder LLMs, and what property earned it that spot?
points: Without positional information, self-attention sees a bag of tokens — "dog bites man" ≡ "man bites dog".
Sinusoidal (fixed, added to embeddings): parameter-free, in-principle extrapolation. Learned absolute: simple, but hard cap at trained length.
Relative biases (ALiBi-style: penalize attention by distance): what matters linguistically is usually offset, not absolute index — and it degrades gracefully past trained length.

RoPE: rotate Q/K pairs by a position-dependent angle so the QK dot product depends only on relative offset — relative behavior without extra bias terms, and amenable to context extension by scaling. The modern decoder default.
Say the meta-point: absolute → relative is the field converging on offset as the right inductive bias.
drill.oneLiner: You inject order via sinusoidal or learned absolute encodings, or relative schemes — and modern LLMs use RoPE, which rotates Q and K so attention scores depend on relative offset.

questions.text: Tokenization — where does it actually bite you?
points: BPE/subword: frequent strings are one token, rare ones fragment
Numbers split unpredictably → arithmetic errors that look like reasoning failures
Non-English and code cost far more tokens → real cost and context penalty per user
Token boundaries break exact matching — a reason sparse retrieval still earns its place
Different tokenizer = different token counts = your cost estimates don't transfer between models
questions.badge: Trending — tokenization-consequence questions recur on LeetCode Discuss + screens (2025–26)
questions.flow: subword merges → rare text fragments → numbers/non-English inflate cost → boundaries break exact match
questions.trap: treating tokens as words when estimating cost or context

drill.prompt: from jbtiq_llm Q3: "Your model can't spell, fails at arithmetic on large numbers, and a user's name gets mangled in French. One root cause connects all three."
drill.badge: Trending — tokenization-consequence questions recur on LeetCode Discuss + screens (2025–26)
drill.hint: The model never sees characters. What does it see, and how does that unit misalign with letters, digits, and non-English text?
points: Root cause: subword tokenization (BPE-family). The model reasons over token IDs, not characters — "strawberry" may be one token, so counting its r's requires knowledge the representation hides. Spelling tasks fail structurally, not from stupidity.

Arithmetic: digit strings segment inconsistently (1234 one token, 12345 split oddly), so positional arithmetic patterns don't align across magnitudes — why digit-level tokenization measurably improves math in models trained that way.

Multilingual inequity: BPE vocabularies are trained on data mixtures dominated by English — French names and non-Latin scripts fragment into many rare tokens → worse representation and more tokens per sentence (higher cost + more context consumed for the same content) for non-English users. That's a product and fairness issue, not a nicety.

Production consequences beyond quality: cost/billing is per token (the same document costs different amounts by language), context budgeting varies by language, and token-boundary artifacts (leading spaces, casing) cause prompt bugs.

The architect's takeaway: tokenizer choice is frozen at pretraining and haunts everything downstream — you can't fix it at inference; you design around it (tools for math, character-level tricks for spelling).
drill.oneLiner: All three are tokenization artifacts — the model sees subword IDs, not characters, so spelling and digit alignment are hidden from it, and English-heavy vocabularies fragment other languages into more, rarer tokens with worse quality and higher cost.

questions.text: What does FlashAttention actually change?
points: Not an approximation — mathematically identical output
The bottleneck was memory bandwidth, not FLOPs: writing the n×n score matrix to HBM
Tiling + online softmax keeps blocks in SRAM; the full matrix is never materialised
Result: big speedup and memory that scales linearly, not quadratically, in practice
This is why long context became affordable — it's a systems win, not a modelling one
questions.badge: Evergreen
questions.flow: score matrix never materialised → tile in SRAM → online softmax → same math, bandwidth-bound fixed
questions.trap: calling it an approximate or sparse attention method

drill.prompt: from jbtiq_dl Q19: "FlashAttention computes exactly the same attention as the naive implementation. So where do the large speedups come from?"
drill.hint: Profile the naive version: is it waiting on arithmetic or on memory? And what n×n object does it write that FlashAttention never does?
points: Attention on GPUs is memory-bandwidth-bound, not FLOP-bound: the naive version materializes the n×n score matrix in HBM, then reads it back for softmax and again for the V product.
FlashAttention tiles Q/K/V blocks into on-chip SRAM and computes softmax online (running max + running sum — the log-sum-exp trick streamed), so the n² matrix never exists in main memory.

It's exact — an IO-aware reordering, not an approximation. Backward pass recomputes attention on the fly instead of storing it → activation memory drops from O(n²) to O(n), unlocking long-context training.
The transferable lesson interviewers want: on modern accelerators, count memory traffic, not FLOPs — kernel fusion beats algorithmic cleverness surprisingly often.
drill.oneLiner: FlashAttention is exact attention reorganized to never materialize the n² matrix — tiled through SRAM with an online softmax — winning because attention is bandwidth-bound, not FLOP-bound.

questions.text: MoE — what's actually sparse?
points: FFN replaced by N experts; a router activates top-k (often 2) per token
Total params huge, active params per token small → capacity without proportional compute
Memory is not saved — all experts must be resident; it's a compute trade, not a memory one
Training pains: load balancing, router collapse, auxiliary losses
Serving pains: expert-parallel routing, uneven utilisation, harder batching
questions.badge: Evergreen
questions.flow: router picks top-k experts per token → total ≫ active → compute saved, memory isn't
questions.trap: "MoE models are smaller" — they need more VRAM, not less

drill.prompt: from jbtiq_dl Q22: "You need roughly 10× model capacity but can't afford 10× inference FLOPs. Walk me through the MoE design — and its two classic failure modes."
drill.hint: Separate parameters stored from parameters active per token. Then think about what must be in memory anyway.
points: Mechanism: FFN layers are replaced by many experts with a learned router sending each token to a small subset (top-k) — so active parameters per token are a fraction of total parameters. Compute (and thus much of the bill) scales with active, not total.
Why it wins: more capacity/knowledge at fixed FLOPs per token — better quality-per-compute at both training and inference, which is why most frontier-scale models went sparse.

The serving catch: all experts must sit in GPU memory — you pay compute for active params but memory for total params; MoE shifts the bottleneck to VRAM and interconnect (expert-parallel all-to-all traffic when experts shard across GPUs).

Operational quirks: load balancing — routers can collapse onto favorite experts (auxiliary balance losses exist for this), batch efficiency depends on tokens distributing across experts, and latency variance rises with routing.
Architect's rule of thumb: MoE is attractive when you're compute-constrained but memory-rich; dense stays attractive for small-footprint deployment and simpler serving.
drill.oneLiner: MoE activates a few experts per token, so you pay compute on active parameters but memory on all of them — quality-per-FLOP goes up while the bottleneck moves to VRAM, interconnect, and router load balance.

questions.text: Scaling laws — what did Chinchilla change?
points: Loss follows a power law in params, data and compute — smooth and predictable
Chinchilla: earlier models were badly undertrained — scale data with params (~20 tokens/param)
Consequence: smaller, longer-trained models beat bigger under-trained ones at equal compute
Inference cost then argues for going further past compute-optimal — you serve far more than you train
"Emergence" is contested — often a metric artefact rather than a phase change
questions.badge: Evergreen
questions.flow: power law → data must scale with params → smaller+longer wins → inference economics push further still
questions.trap: quoting emergent abilities as settled fact

drill.prompt: from jbtiq_dl Q33: "Fixed compute budget: do you train a bigger model or feed more tokens? How do you actually reason about it?"
drill.hint: What do scaling laws actually predict smoothly, what appears to jump, and what's the measurement critique of the jumps?
points: Scaling laws: loss falls smoothly and predictably as a power law in parameters, data, and compute — the Chinchilla insight being that for a compute budget, models were undertrained on data (parameters and tokens should scale together). That predictability is why frontier training runs are financeable at all.

"Emergence" — capabilities appearing suddenly at scale — is real as a user experience but contested as a measurement: sharp jumps often reflect discontinuous metrics (exact-match scoring makes gradual improvement look like a phase change); smoother metrics show smoother gains. Say both sides.

The honest CTO framing: downstream capability at the task you care about is not reliably predictable from loss curves — which is why evals on your task, not benchmark headlines, drive adoption decisions.

Current-era nuance: pure parameter scaling has diminishing economics — the frontier moved to data quality, post-training, and test-time compute (reasoning models trade inference tokens for capability), a second scaling axis with direct serving-cost implications.
Implication for strategy: plan for capability step-changes arriving via new model generations regardless of your roadmap — architecture that swaps models cheaply captures that upside.
drill.oneLiner: Loss scales predictably — that's what makes training runs financeable — but task-level capability doesn't map cleanly from loss, emergence is partly a metric artifact, and the modern gains come as much from data quality, post-training, and test-time compute as from parameters.

questions.text: Temperature, top-p, top-k — what do you set for what?
points: Logits → temperature divides before softmax: <1 sharpens, >1 flattens
top-k = fixed count · top-p (nucleus) = smallest set covering probability mass p — adapts to confidence
Extraction / tool args / classification → temperature 0 or near it
Creative / diverse candidates → higher temp + top-p ~0.9
Repetition penalties are a blunt patch for degeneration, not a quality dial
questions.badge: Evergreen
questions.flow: temp shapes the distribution → top-p adapts the cut → deterministic tasks near 0, generative higher
questions.trap: raising temperature to "make it smarter" — it makes it less likely, not more correct

drill.prompt: from jbtiq_llm Q12: "Temperature, top-p, top-k — what does each mathematically do, and give me your settings for: a JSON extractor, a support bot, and a creative writer."
drill.hint: One reshapes the distribution, two truncate it — by different criteria. Settings follow from how much of the tail each task can tolerate.
points: Temperature rescales logits before softmax: T<1 sharpens toward the mode, T>1 flattens toward uniform, T→0 approaches greedy. It reshapes; it never removes options.

Top-k truncates to the k highest-probability tokens (fixed count, blind to how peaked the distribution is); top-p (nucleus) truncates to the smallest set whose cumulative mass ≥ p — adaptive: narrow when the model is confident, wide when uncertain. That adaptivity is why top-p aged better than top-k.

Settings with reasons: JSON extractor → T≈0 (determinism and schema fidelity beat diversity; ideally constrained decoding does the guaranteeing). Support bot → low-moderate T (~0.3–0.7 territory) — natural variation without policy-adjacent creativity, plus guardrails doing the real safety work. Creative writer → higher T with top-p — diversity is the product; the tail is where the interesting tokens live.

Two caveats that mark seniority: T=0 does not guarantee reproducibility across serving stacks (batching and floating-point nondeterminism), and sampling parameters are shipped configuration — version them with the prompt, because a silent temperature change is a silent behavior change.
Greedy/beam search sit at the deterministic end — beam helps constrained tasks like translation and hurts open-ended generation (repetitive, degenerate text).
drill.oneLiner: Temperature reshapes the distribution, top-k truncates by count, top-p truncates by adaptive mass — so the extractor runs near-zero with constrained decoding, the support bot runs low with guardrails, the writer runs hot with nucleus sampling, and all of it is versioned config.

questions.text: Temperature is 0 but output still varies. Why?
points: Temperature 0 is greedy — but greedy isn't bit-reproducible on a GPU
Floating-point non-associativity: batching and kernel scheduling change reduction order
Different batch composition → different numerics → a different argmax on a near-tie
MoE routing, speculative decoding and provider-side model updates add more variance
Design for it: seeds where offered, tolerance-based tests, never assert exact string equality
questions.flow: greedy ≠ deterministic → FP reduction order varies with batching → near-ties flip
questions.trap: promising reproducibility because you set temperature to 0

questions.text: How do you force valid JSON out of a model?
points: Constrain decoding, don't post-hoc parse — mask logits to only tokens the grammar allows
Provider structured outputs / JSON schema mode is the same idea, server-side
Guarantees syntactic validity only — semantic correctness still needs your validation
Cost: constraint machinery, some quality loss if the schema fights the model's natural phrasing
Failure path: bounded repair prompt, then fail loudly — never silently coerce
questions.flow: schema → constrained decode → valid syntax → still validate semantics → bounded repair
questions.trap: conflating "parses" with "correct"

questions.text: What can you do with logprobs?
points: Per-token log-probability — a confidence-ish signal, cheap and already there
Uses: abstention thresholds, routing to a bigger model, flagging spans for review, classification via option scores
Big caveat: models are poorly calibrated — confident and wrong is the normal failure
Sequence-level needs length normalisation or long answers always look uncertain
Not available from every provider — don't design a system that requires them
questions.badge: Trending — logprob-engineering questions recur in LLM-platform JDs (2025–26)
questions.flow: token logprobs → normalise → threshold for abstain/escalate → but calibration is weak
questions.trap: treating logprob as probability-of-correct

drill.prompt: from jbtiq_llm Q13: "What can you build with logprobs that you can't build without them?"
drill.badge: Trending — logprob-engineering questions recur in LLM-platform JDs (2025–26)
drill.hint: They're the model's per-token confidence. Think: classification, uncertainty routing, and detection use cases.
points: Calibrated-ish classification for free: for label tasks, read the logprobs of the label tokens instead of parsing generated text — you get a score, not just a choice, enabling thresholds and abstention ("route to human below X confidence").

Uncertainty-based routing and escalation: low sequence-level likelihood or a flat token distribution flags shaky generations — trigger retrieval, a bigger model, or human review selectively instead of uniformly paying for the expensive path.

Hallucination heuristics: low-confidence spans inside a fluent answer correlate (imperfectly) with fabrication — useful as a signal into verification pipelines, not as a detector on its own; and perplexity-under-the-model supports drift detection on inputs.

Eval plumbing: score multiple-choice benchmarks by comparing option likelihoods (no parsing fragility), compare prompt variants by likelihood of gold outputs, and detect distribution shift in production traffic.

Constraints to name: chat APIs expose logprobs unevenly, post-trained models are systematically overconfident (calibration eroded by preference tuning), so raw probabilities need recalibration before you treat them as probabilities.
drill.oneLiner: Logprobs turn generation into scored prediction — label classification with abstention thresholds, uncertainty-based routing to bigger models or humans, and weak-but-useful hallucination and drift signals — remembering post-trained models are overconfident, so calibrate before trusting the numbers.

questions.text: Walk the post-training stack.
points: Pretrain (next token) → SFT (instruction following) → preference optimisation (RLHF/DPO) → optional reasoning post-training
SFT teaches format and task; preference tuning teaches which of two answers people prefer
Each stage is smaller and more expensive per example than the last
Reward hacking / specification gaming is the recurring failure of the preference stage
Most product problems are solved at prompt or SFT level — not by RL
questions.badge: Trending — the post-training stack is a staple of LLM screens (2025–26)
questions.flow: pretrain → SFT for behaviour → preference for ranking → reasoning tuning last
questions.trap: describing RLHF as where the model "learns facts"

drill.prompt: from jbtiq_llm Q8: "SFT → RLHF → DPO: what does each stage actually change in the model, and why did DPO become the default first move?"
drill.badge: Trending — the post-training stack is a staple of LLM screens (2025–26)
drill.hint: One stage teaches format, one optimizes against a learned judge, one skips the judge. Where does the instability live?
points: SFT: supervised next-token training on curated (instruction, response) pairs — teaches format and behavior (chat style, instruction following). It imitates; it can't express "this answer is better than that one".

RLHF: fit a reward model on human preference pairs, then RL (PPO-style) optimizes the policy against it with a KL penalty anchoring to the SFT model. Powerful but operationally heavy: four models in memory, RL instability, and vulnerability to reward hacking — the policy exploits reward-model gaps (verbosity, sycophancy, confident tone) rather than getting better.

DPO: a closed-form reformulation — optimize preference pairs directly with a classification-style loss, no explicit reward model, no RL loop. Stable, cheap, reproducible → the default first move for preference tuning; the trade is less flexibility than online RL (no exploration, quality capped by the static preference set).

The current-era addendum: reasoning post-training — RL against verifiable rewards (math checkers, unit tests) rather than learned preference models — sidesteps reward hacking where verifiers exist and produced the reasoning-model generation.

Say the failure vocabulary: reward hacking and specification gaming are Goodhart's law applied to a learned metric — the reward model is a proxy, and hard optimization against any proxy eventually optimizes the gap.
drill.oneLiner: SFT teaches format by imitation, RLHF optimizes against a learned reward with all the instability and reward-hacking that implies, and DPO gets most of the preference gain as a stable supervised loss — with the frontier now adding RL against verifiable rewards where checkers exist.

questions.text: RLHF or DPO?
points: RLHF: train a reward model, then PPO against it — powerful, unstable, expensive, many moving parts
DPO: optimise the preference objective directly on pairs — no reward model, no RL loop, far simpler
DPO is the default now for most teams; RLHF retains an edge where online exploration matters
Both need good preference data — that's the real cost, not the algorithm
Variants (IPO, KTO, ORPO) trade off overfitting to preferences and data format
questions.flow: preferences → reward model + PPO (RLHF) or direct objective on pairs (DPO) → data is the real cost
questions.trap: framing it as accuracy — the differences are stability, cost and complexity

questions.text: How does LoRA work, and why is it cheap?
points: Freeze base weights; learn a low-rank update ΔW = B·A with rank r ≪ d
Trainable params drop by orders of magnitude → optimiser state and memory collapse with them
Merged at inference → zero added latency, or kept separate to swap adapters
Dials: rank r, alpha, and which modules (attention projections typically)
Wrong tool for new knowledge — it adapts behaviour and style, not facts (see #17)
questions.badge: Trending — LoRA mechanics are a fixture of LLM screens (2025–26)
questions.flow: freeze base → learn low-rank delta → tiny optimiser state → merge or hot-swap
questions.trap: proposing LoRA to inject fresh domain knowledge — that's a retrieval problem

drill.prompt: from jbtiq_llm Q10: "LoRA: the mechanism, why it works, and the serving superpower nobody mentions in tutorials."
drill.badge: Trending — LoRA mechanics are a fixture of LLM screens (2025–26)
drill.hint: What's the assumption about the rank of the weight update? And at serving time, what can you do with many adapters that you can't do with many full fine-tunes?
points: Mechanism: freeze W, learn the update as a low-rank factorization ΔW = BA (rank r ≪ d), injected into attention/FFN projections; train only A and B — a tiny fraction of parameters, dramatically less optimizer memory (which, not gradient compute, is what makes full fine-tuning expensive).

Why it works: task adaptation empirically lives in a low-dimensional subspace of weight space — you rarely need full-rank freedom to shift behavior; r is the capacity dial (too low underfits the adaptation, higher approaches full FT).
QLoRA extends the memory win: quantize the frozen base to 4-bit, train LoRA on top with a paged optimizer — single-GPU fine-tuning of large models, quality close to full-precision fine-tunes.

The serving superpower: adapters are small and hot-swappable — merge into weights for zero overhead, or serve many adapters over one shared base (batched multi-adapter serving), which makes per-tenant/per-task customization economically sane: one base model in VRAM, hundreds of personalities.

Honest limits: LoRA shines for style/format/domain behavior; it's weaker for injecting large bodies of new knowledge (that's continued pretraining or RAG territory), and adapter quality depends on which modules you target.
drill.oneLiner: LoRA learns the weight update as a low-rank product on a frozen base — betting that adaptation lives in a small subspace — which slashes training memory, and at serving time adapters merge to zero overhead or multiplex hundreds of tenants over one base model.

questions.text: QLoRA — what's the trick?
points: Base model quantised to 4-bit (NF4), frozen; LoRA adapters trained in higher precision on top
Gradients flow through the quantised base without updating it
Double quantisation + paged optimisers cut memory further — big models on one GPU
Cost: some quality loss, slower per step than fp16 LoRA
Enables fine-tuning at a hardware tier that otherwise couldn't hold the model
questions.flow: 4-bit frozen base → backprop through it → train fp16 adapters → single-GPU fine-tune
questions.trap: implying the deployed model must stay quantised — adapters can merge into a full-precision base

questions.text: Fine-tuning made it worse at everything else. What happened?
points: Catastrophic forgetting — narrow data overwrites general capability
Worse with full fine-tuning, high LR, many epochs, small homogeneous datasets
Mitigations: PEFT/LoRA (base frozen), mix in general data, low LR, early stop, fewer epochs
Evaluate on a held-out general benchmark, not just your task — or you won't see it
Often the real lesson: the task needed retrieval or prompting, not weights
questions.badge: Evergreen
questions.flow: narrow data + full FT → general ability degrades → freeze base, mix data, eval broadly
questions.trap: measuring only task accuracy and declaring the fine-tune a success

drill.prompt: from jbtiq_llm Q9: "After fine-tuning on your domain data, the model is better at your task and noticeably dumber at everything else. What happened and what are the controls?"
drill.hint: The weights that moved were load-bearing for other behaviors. Name the phenomenon and three mitigations across data, method, and evaluation.
points: Catastrophic forgetting: gradient updates for the narrow task overwrite representations serving general capabilities — the narrower and longer the fine-tune, the worse the erosion; instruction-following and safety behaviors are often the first casualties.

Data controls: mix replay data (general instruction data blended with domain data), keep the fine-tune short and low-LR, and question the premise — if the knowledge is factual, RAG beats fine-tuning and forgets nothing.

Method controls: PEFT/LoRA — freezing base weights structurally limits what can be forgotten (adapters nudge, not overwrite); regularization toward the base model (KL/weight anchoring) for full fine-tunes.

Evaluation control — the one teams skip: hold a general-capability regression suite (instruction following, reasoning, safety probes) next to your task eval, and gate the fine-tune on both. Improvement on your metric with silent regression elsewhere is the default outcome, not the exception.
Decision framing: fine-tune for behavior/format/domain style, RAG for knowledge, prompting for cheap wins first — reach for weights last.
drill.oneLiner: That's catastrophic forgetting — narrow gradients overwrote general behavior — controlled by replay mixtures, LoRA-style frozen bases, short low-LR runs, and a general regression suite gating the release; and if the goal was knowledge rather than behavior, RAG was the right tool anyway.

questions.text: What is in-context learning actually doing?
points: No weights change — examples condition the forward pass, nothing is learned persistently
Format and label space matter more than label correctness in many findings
Sensitive to example order, count and recency — a real source of prompt brittleness
Costs tokens on every call; heavy few-shot is a recurring hidden cost line
Once examples get numerous and stable, that's the signal to consider SFT
questions.badge: Evergreen
questions.flow: examples condition the pass → format carries most of the signal → per-call cost → many stable examples → SFT
questions.trap: calling it learning — nothing persists past the request

drill.prompt: from jbtiq_llm Q19: "Few-shot examples: what is the model actually 'learning' in-context — and what do the examples control that instructions can't?"
drill.hint: No weights change. So what mechanism makes examples work, and which properties of the examples carry the signal?
points: No learning in the gradient sense — the forward pass conditions on the examples; the mainstream account is task location and format induction: examples activate behavior the pretrained model already has and pin down the output distribution's shape.

The evidence that shapes practice: format, label space, and input distribution of the examples matter enormously — sometimes more than label correctness; examples are unmatched at conveying "output looks exactly like this" where prose instructions stay ambiguous.

Practical handles: order effects are real (recency bias — the last example pulls hardest), diverse examples beat redundant ones, hard/boundary cases teach more than easy ones, and few-shot pairs beautifully with structured output (show the exact JSON).

Costs: examples eat context and per-request tokens forever — prompt caching neutralizes the latency/cost hit for static example blocks; and for well-post-trained models on common tasks, zero-shot with a crisp instruction often matches few-shot — measure before paying.
The senior habit: treat example sets like code — versioned, evaluated (add/remove and re-run the eval), and curated from real failure cases rather than invented.
drill.oneLiner: In-context examples don't update weights — they locate the task and pin the output format, which is why their format and distribution matter as much as their correctness — so I use them where instructions are ambiguous, cache them, and version them like code.

questions.text: Reasoning models and test-time compute — what changed?
points: Spend more compute at inference: long chains, sampling, verification, search
Trained to use that budget well (reasoning post-training), not just prompted to
Buys accuracy on maths, code and multi-step logic; buys nothing on retrieval or formatting tasks
New cost/latency profile: reasoning tokens you pay for and often never show the user
Architect judgement: route by task — reasoning model only where the task actually needs it
questions.badge: Trending — CoT-vs-reasoning-models recurs across screens (2025–26)
questions.flow: more inference compute → better multi-step accuracy → but latency + hidden token cost → route selectively
questions.trap: defaulting everything to a reasoning model and watching cost and TTFT triple

drill.prompt: from jbtiq_llm Q20: "Chain-of-thought and test-time compute: when does 'think step by step' help, when does it hurt, and what did reasoning models change about the trade?"
drill.hint: CoT helps a specific problem shape. It hurts two things categorically. And reasoning models moved the dial from prompt to parameter.
points: Helps on multi-step problems with intermediate state — math, logic, multi-hop analysis — by externalizing computation into tokens (each step conditions the next; depth the forward pass lacks gets bought as sequence length). Self-consistency (sample multiple chains, majority-vote) adds accuracy where answers are checkable/discrete.

Hurts: latency and cost always (more tokens); accuracy on tasks where verbalizing degrades performance (some classification/perception tasks); and the chains themselves are not faithful explanations — plausible-sounding reasoning can decorate a wrong (or right) answer, so never sell CoT text as an audit trail.

Reasoning models internalized the pattern: extended deliberation trained in via RL on verifiable problems, with thinking budgets as an API parameter — test-time compute became a dial you buy (quality vs latency/cost) rather than a prompt trick, and "think step by step" adds little on top.

The production decision it created: routing by problem difficulty — standard model for the easy 90%, reasoning budget for the hard 10% — since paying thinking-tokens on trivial requests is pure waste.
Say the eval discipline: measure whether added thinking actually improves your task before paying for it — on retrieval-answerable or format tasks it often doesn't.
drill.oneLiner: CoT buys serial depth with tokens — worth it on multi-step problems, pure cost on easy ones, and never a faithful audit trail — and reasoning models turned that trick into a purchasable thinking budget, making difficulty-based routing the real production skill.

questions.text: Why do models hallucinate?
points: The objective is plausibility, not truth — a fluent guess scores like a fluent fact
Separate the two: factuality (true in the world) vs faithfulness (true to the given context)
RAG targets faithfulness; it does not fix factuality when retrieval misses
Amplifiers: no abstention path, long context dilution, sycophancy from preference tuning
Mitigations stack: retrieval + citation + abstention + verification — no single one is enough

links.label: Hallucination causes & factuality vs faithfulness
links.target: 05-LLM-Production/11-Hallucination, Safety & Guardrails/01-Hallucination causes & factuality vs faithfulness

questions.badge: Evergreen — the definitional question that still filters candidates.
questions.flow: trained for plausibility → split factuality vs faithfulness → RAG helps the second → add abstention + verify
questions.trap: promising RAG "solves hallucination"

drill.prompt: from jbtiq_llm Q24: "Why do LLMs hallucinate — mechanistically, not morally? Distinguish factuality from faithfulness while you're at it."
drill.badge: Evergreen — the definitional question that still filters candidates.
drill.hint: Start from the training objective: what is the model optimized to produce? And the two terms differ by what the output is checked against.
points: Mechanistic causes: the objective optimizes plausible continuation, not truth — likelihood rewards fluent, confident text; the model has no fact/fiction boundary in its representations. Add: knowledge gaps filled by interpolation (rare entities, post-cutoff events), exposure/decoding effects (sampling can commit to a wrong token early and rationalize onward), and post-training that historically rewarded confident answers over "I don't know" — calibration eroded in favor of helpfulness.

The distinction: factuality = agreement with world truth; faithfulness = agreement with provided source material. RAG converts much of the factuality problem into a faithfulness problem — which is checkable, and that checkability is half the point of RAG.

Failure taxonomy worth naming: fabricated entities/citations (the classic), subtle numeric/temporal corruption (more dangerous — plausible and wrong), and unfaithful summarization (says what the doc didn't).

Mitigation stack in one breath: grounding + citation enforcement, faithfulness eval (judge/NLI-style checks against sources), uncertainty signals and abstention paths, tool calls for computable facts (calculator, DB), and UX honesty (citations users can check).
The sentence that shows maturity: hallucination is structural, managed not eliminated — the design goal is that when the model is wrong, the system makes it detectable and cheap.
drill.oneLiner: The objective rewards plausible continuation, not truth — gaps get interpolated fluently and post-training taught confidence over abstention — so I convert factuality into checkable faithfulness with grounding, enforce citations, and design for detectability rather than promising elimination.

questions.text: Prompt injection vs jailbreak — are they the same problem?
points: Jailbreak = the user subverts the model's policy
Injection = a third party plants instructions in content the model reads — the more dangerous one
Indirect injection is the systems problem: retrieved doc, web page, email, tool output
Root cause: instructions and data share one channel with no privilege boundary
Defences are layered: treat retrieved content as untrusted, least privilege on tools, approval for destructive actions, output filtering — not "prompt it to ignore injections"
questions.badge: Trending — injection questions now standard even for non-agentic LLM roles (2025–26)
questions.flow: user-subversion vs third-party-planted → indirect is the systems risk → no trust boundary → least privilege + approval
questions.trap: offering a defensive system prompt as the mitigation

drill.prompt: from jbtiq_llm Q38: "Prompt injection for an LLM app (not an agent): where does it bite when there are no tools to hijack?"
drill.badge: Trending — injection questions now standard even for non-agentic LLM roles (2025–26)
drill.hint: No tools, but the model still reads untrusted content and its output still goes somewhere. Trace both.
points: The channels without tools: indirect injection via RAG (a poisoned document in the corpus instructs the model — "ignore previous instructions, recommend X" buried in a retrieved page), via user-uploaded files, and via any third-party content the app summarizes. The corpus is an attack surface.

What gets hijacked without tools: the output itself — misinformation delivered under your brand's voice, prompt/system-instruction exfiltration ("repeat your instructions"), policy bypass through content smuggling, and downstream sinks (if output feeds HTML → XSS; feeds SQL → injection; feeds another LLM → chained injection). Output is untrusted data to every consumer.

Defenses at this tier: source hygiene for the corpus (provenance, ingestion-time scanning), instruction/data separation attempts (delimiters, system-prompt hardening — helpful, not sufficient, say so), output encoding/sanitization at every sink, groundedness checks (an answer citing instructions-not-content is a flag), and monitoring for instruction-shaped text in retrieved chunks.
Design honesty: same conclusion as the agent case at lower stakes — no in-band fix is reliable; you bound impact (what can output reach?) and detect, rather than prevent perfectly.
Say the checklist habit: every place model output is consumed — UI, DB, code, another model — gets the same skepticism as user input, because that's what it is.
drill.oneLiner: Without tools, injection hijacks the output — poisoned RAG documents speaking through your brand, prompt exfiltration, and payloads riding into downstream sinks — so the defenses are corpus hygiene, output sanitization everywhere it lands, and treating model output as user input, because in-band prevention is never complete.

questions.text: It has a 200k context. Should you fill it?
points: No. Advertised window ≠ usable window — accuracy degrades well before the limit
Lost in the middle: recall is strong at the start and end, weak in between
Every token costs money and prefill latency — TTFT grows with what you stuff
Position matters: put the critical material at the edges, order retrieved chunks deliberately
Long context and RAG are complements — retrieve well, then fill sparingly
questions.badge: Trending — long-context-vs-RAG recurs everywhere (2025–26)
questions.flow: usable ≪ advertised → middle degrades → cost + TTFT scale with fill → retrieve, then place deliberately
questions.trap: treating a large window as a reason to skip retrieval

drill.prompt: from jbtiq_llm Q17: "A million-token context window: what does it actually cost, what does the model actually do with it, and when is it the wrong tool?"
drill.hint: Three angles: the compute/memory bill, the utilization research finding, and the comparison against retrieval.
points: The bill: prefill compute grows quadratically with context, KV cache grows linearly — a maxed-out window means slow TTFT and a cache that crowds out batch concurrency; per-request cost scales with tokens whether or not they mattered.

Utilization reality: effective use is uneven — lost-in-the-middle (information buried mid-context is recalled worse than at the edges), and long-context benchmarks (needle-in-haystack and beyond) show retrieval ≠ reasoning over the full window; claimed length and usable length differ by task.

Wrong tool when: the corpus is larger than any window, changes frequently (re-prefilling a million tokens per query is absurd — retrieval indexes update incrementally), needs access control (RAG filters per user; a stuffed context can't), or when you need citations/auditability.
Right tool when: genuinely holistic reads (whole-codebase reasoning, full-contract analysis, long-session agents) where cross-references span everything and chunking destroys the object.

The production pattern is both: retrieve to select, long context to reason over the selection generously — plus prompt caching for the stable prefix; and KV-offloading tricks blur the boundary further.
drill.oneLiner: Long context pays quadratic prefill and linear KV for tokens the model may under-use — lost-in-the-middle is real — so retrieval still owns large, fresh, access-controlled corpora, long context owns holistic reads, and production uses retrieval to select then a generous window to reason.

questions.text: How do models get extended to long context at all?
points: Training at full length is quadratic and unaffordable — extension is mostly post-hoc
RoPE scaling — position interpolation, NTK-aware, YaRN — stretch the rotation, then briefly fine-tune
Architectural routes: sliding-window/restricted attention, and SSM/linear-attention hybrids (Mamba)
Systems routes: FlashAttention (#6), KV paging and offload (#3)
Always ask what the effective context is, not the advertised one (#22)
questions.badge: Evergreen (mechanism check behind the long-context marketing)
questions.flow: can't train long → scale RoPE + short fine-tune → plus restricted attention and KV systems work
questions.trap: assuming a bigger advertised window was trained at that length

drill.prompt: from jbtiq_llm Q35: "Context extension: the model was trained at 8k — what makes it work at 128k, and why doesn't it 'just work'?"
drill.badge: Evergreen (mechanism check behind the long-context marketing)
drill.hint: What breaks is the model's sense of position. How is position encoded in modern models, and what do the extension tricks rescale?
points: The core problem: positional encodings — modern models use RoPE (rotary embeddings encoding relative position as rotation angles) — are only trained over the pretraining length; beyond it, attention sees angle combinations it never learned → out-of-distribution positions, quality collapse.

Extension methods rescale the geometry: position interpolation (compress new positions into the trained range), NTK-aware/frequency-based scaling (rescale RoPE frequencies non-uniformly — high frequencies preserved for local precision, low frequencies stretched for range — the YaRN-family refinement), typically followed by continued pretraining on long sequences to adapt.

Why it doesn't "just work": interpolation without fine-tuning blurs positional resolution (nearby-token discrimination suffers); and even adapted models show uneven utilization across the window — trained length vs advertised length vs effectively usable length are three different numbers.

The data problem behind the compute problem: genuinely long, coherent training documents are scarce — much long-context training is synthetic or concatenated, which shapes what "long-range skill" the model really has (retrieval across the window ≠ reasoning across it).

Practical consequence: evaluate long-context claims on your task shape (multi-document synthesis, cross-referencing) rather than needle-in-a-haystack, which is nearly saturated and tests the easiest skill.
drill.oneLiner: Extension is mostly RoPE geometry surgery — interpolating or frequency-rescaling positions into the trained range, then continued pretraining on long sequences — and it doesn't 'just work' because positional resolution and mid-window utilization degrade, making usable length shorter than advertised length.

questions.text: Fine-tune, RAG, or prompt — for this problem?
points: Ask what you're injecting: knowledge → RAG · behaviour/format → fine-tune · one document → long context
Knowledge that changes, is large, or needs citation is never a fine-tuning problem
Cost shapes differ: RAG per query · FT once + every refresh · long context every token every call
Usual production answer: RAG + a tuned embedding model, not a tuned LLM
Cross-ref [[05-RAG]] #2 — same decision from the retrieval side

questions.badge: Trending — the canonical "when to fine-tune" question, still everywhere (2025–26)
questions.flow: what am I injecting? → knowledge RAG · behaviour FT · single doc LC → usually RAG + tuned embeddings
questions.trap: "fine-tune it on our docs" — it learns form, not facts

drill.prompt: from jbtiq_llm Q11: "Prompting vs RAG vs LoRA vs full fine-tuning vs continued pretraining — give me the decision procedure you'd defend in an architecture review."
drill.badge: Trending — the canonical "when to fine-tune" question, still everywhere (2025–26)
drill.hint: Sort by what you're trying to change: knowledge, behavior, or capability — and by iteration speed and reversibility.
points: The sorting question: what needs to change? Knowledge (facts, documents, freshness) → RAG — updatable, auditable, citable, no forgetting. Behavior (format, tone, task style, domain dialect) → prompting first, LoRA when prompt length/consistency/cost make prompts untenable. Capability (fundamentally new skills, deep domain language) → continued pretraining / full FT — the expensive last resort.

Secondary axes that decide ties: iteration speed (prompt changes ship in minutes, fine-tunes in days), reversibility (prompts and adapters roll back trivially), data reality (fine-tuning needs thousands of quality examples — most teams don't have them and should hear that), and evaluation cost (every weight change needs the regression suite).

Escalation discipline: exhaust prompting (+ few-shot + prompt caching to kill the cost argument) → add RAG for knowledge → LoRA for behavior at scale → full FT/continued pretraining only with a measured gap, a real dataset, and an eval harness.
Anti-pattern to name: fine-tuning to inject facts — it's lossy, unauditable, ages instantly, and forgets other things while doing it.
These compose: production systems are typically prompt + RAG + (sometimes) a LoRA — it's not a menu of one.
drill.oneLiner: Change knowledge with RAG, behavior with prompts then LoRA, capability with heavier training — escalating only on measured gaps, because prompts iterate in minutes and roll back for free, and fine-tuning facts into weights is the canonical anti-pattern.

questions.text: Where have you had to reason about model behaviour, not just call an API?
points: Pick a moment the model itself was the variable — tokenizer cost, context degradation, decoding config, a bad fine-tune
Name the observable symptom before the explanation
The measurement that isolated it to model behaviour rather than your code
The lever you chose — decoding, context placement, model swap, routing — and the one you rejected
Number: quality, cost or latency, before → after
questions.flow: symptom → isolate to model behaviour → lever chosen + rejected → number
questions.trap: a purely conceptual answer with no system you actually touched

questions.text: 🗣️ (jbtiq_llm Q6 · S3 Pretraining) "Perplexity: what does it measure, when is it the right metric, and when is a lower perplexity model worse for you?
points: Definition worth saying precisely: exponentiated average negative log-likelihood per token — intuitively, the effective branching factor: "how many tokens was the model choosing among on average". Lower = better next-token prediction on that corpus.
It's the right metric for pretraining progress on a held-out slice of the training distribution, comparing checkpoints of the same tokenizer and data recipe.

Traps: perplexity is not comparable across tokenizers (different token counts change per-token averages), and it's corpus-relative — a model can hold lower perplexity on web text yet be worse at your legal-domain task, instruction following, or safety. Post-trained chat models can show worse perplexity while being far more useful.
Also blind to what you actually ship: hallucination rates, tool-use reliability, refusal behavior — none visible in perplexity.
The senior sentence: perplexity is a thermometer for pretraining, not a report card for products — task evals decide adoption.
questions.badge: Evergreen
questions.oneLiner: Perplexity is exponentiated per-token negative log-likelihood — the model's average branching factor on a given corpus — great for tracking pretraining, incomparable across tokenizers, and silent about instruction-following, factuality, and your task.

questions.text: 🗣️ (jbtiq_llm Q7 · S3 Pretraining) "Data pipeline for a pretraining run: what are the stages, and which two failures poison the model permanently?
points: Stages: acquisition (web crawls, code, books, licensed sets) → quality filtering (classifier- and heuristic-based junk removal) → deduplication (exact + near-dup at document and n-gram level) → mixture design (domain weights — code %, multilingual %, etc. — a first-class hyperparameter that shapes downstream ability) → curriculum/ordering decisions.

Poison #1 — benchmark contamination: eval sets leaking into training data inflate scores invisibly; you lose the ability to measure your own model. Decontamination against known evals is now table stakes, and the paranoia extends to your own held-out sets.

Poison #2 — PII and memorizable secrets: models regurgitate rare, repeated strings (keys, personal data) — a privacy/legal exposure baked in at training time; dedup is also the main memorization mitigation, since repetition drives regurgitation.

Quality beats quantity in the current era: aggressive filtering + dedup on a smaller corpus outperforms raw scale — the "data wall" pushed frontier effort into curation and synthetic data, with model-collapse risk (training on your own outputs) as the new failure to manage.
Architect relevance even if you never pretrain: the same discipline applies to fine-tuning corpora — contamination, dedup, PII scrubbing, mixture weights — at a scale you will own.

links.label: Privacy — memorization, PII extraction & data governance
links.target: 05-LLM-Production/11-Hallucination, Safety & Guardrails/07-Privacy — memorization, PII extraction & data governance

questions.badge: Trending — data-quality questions recur in LLM-engineer JDs (2025–26)
questions.oneLiner: Filter, dedup, and mix — with the two permanent poisons being benchmark contamination, which blinds your own evals, and repeated PII, which the model will memorize and regurgitate; dedup is quietly the main defense against both memorization and wasted compute.

questions.text: 🗣️ (jbtiq_llm Q18 · S8 Long Context & Memory) "Mamba, SSMs, linear attention — why do these architectures keep almost winning, and what keeps transformers on top?
points: The pitch: attention is O(n²) with a KV cache that grows with context; SSMs/Mamba process sequences with a fixed-size recurrent state — linear-time training, constant memory per token at inference, no KV cache growth. For long sequences and streaming, the serving economics are structurally better.

The catch: a fixed-size state is lossy compression of the past — precise random-access recall (find the exact quote, copy a variable name from 50k tokens back) is exactly what attention does natively and compressed states struggle with; in-context learning fidelity historically lagged.

The equilibrium that emerged: hybrids — mostly-SSM/linear layers with a few full-attention layers interleaved — capturing most of the efficiency while retaining recall; production-scale hybrid models exist, but the transformer's ecosystem moat (tooling, serving stacks, operator maturity, sunk optimization like FlashAttention/PagedAttention) keeps it the default.

Architect's read: watch cost-per-quality trends rather than picking a religious side — if your workload is long-context-heavy and recall-light (streaming logs, audio, agents with external memory), these architectures shift the economics first there.
questions.badge: Evergreen (the architecture-literacy probe)
questions.oneLiner: Linear-time architectures replace the growing KV cache with a fixed compressed state — great economics, weaker exact recall over long ranges — so hybrids with a few attention layers are the practical convergence, and the transformer's real moat right now is its optimization ecosystem.

questions.text: 🗣️ (jbtiq_llm Q22 · S10 Evaluation) "Why is LLM evaluation fundamentally harder than classical ML evaluation — and what does a production eval stack look like because of it?
points: What breaks: open-ended outputs (many valid answers — no exact-match label), multidimensional quality (an answer can be fluent, relevant, and factually wrong — one score lies), and distribution instability (benchmark contamination, prompt sensitivity, model updates shifting behavior under you).
Benchmarks are weak evidence for your product: contamination inflates them, they saturate, and headline scores don't transfer to your domain — the architect's rule is your task, your data, your eval.

The production stack layers: programmatic assertions where possible (schema, must-contain, tests pass — cheap, deterministic) → LLM-as-judge with rubrics for the fuzzy dimensions, calibrated against human labels and audited for its biases (verbosity, position, self-preference) → human review sampled where judgment is expensive → online signals (task completion, edits, complaints, A/B) as ground truth.
Separate the dimensions explicitly — factuality, instruction-following, reasoning, safety evaluated as different suites — because a single "quality" number hides which one regressed.
The flywheel again: production failures → triaged → eval cases; the golden set is grown, not authored in a workshop.

links.label: Evaluating reasoning, factuality & instruction following separately

questions.badge: Trending — the eval-philosophy opener across LLM JDs (2025–26)
questions.oneLiner: Open-ended outputs, multidimensional quality, and unstable distributions break the one-prediction-one-label paradigm — so the stack layers programmatic checks, calibrated LLM judges per quality dimension, sampled human review, and online signals, all fed by triaged production failures.

questions.text: 🗣️ (jbtiq_llm Q23 · S10 Evaluation) "LLM-as-judge: which biases are documented, and how do you make a judge trustworthy enough to gate releases?
points: Documented biases: position bias (favoring the first/last option in pairwise comparison — mitigate by swapping orders and averaging), verbosity bias (longer answers score higher at equal quality), self-preference (models favor their own family's outputs — don't judge a model with itself), and sycophancy toward confident tone. Rubric vagueness amplifies all of them.

Making it trustworthy: calibrate against human labels — measure judge-human agreement on a labeled sample (and human-human agreement as the ceiling); if the judge can't match human consistency, it can't gate releases. Re-calibrate when the judge model or rubric changes.

Design for reliability: specific rubrics with anchored scales (described levels, not "rate 1–10"), decomposed criteria judged separately (faithfulness separately from completeness), reference-guided judging where a gold answer exists, and pairwise comparison over absolute scoring when ranking is what you need.

Operational guards: version the judge (model + prompt + rubric) like any component, audit a sample of judgments continuously, and watch for drift between judge scores and online outcomes — a judge that diverges from user reality is optimizing you toward the wrong target.
The framing sentence: a judge is a learned metric — Goodhart applies; treat its score as a proxy under continuous audit, not as truth.
questions.badge: Trending — judge-reliability questions recur on LeetCode Discuss + JDs (2025–26)
questions.oneLiner: Judges carry position, verbosity, and self-preference biases — so anchor the rubric, swap orders, decompose criteria, calibrate against human agreement before letting it gate anything, and keep auditing it against online outcomes, because a judge is a learned metric and Goodhart never sleeps.

questions.text: 🗣️ (jbtiq_llm Q25 · S11 Hallucination, Safety & Guardrails) "Design the content-safety pipeline for a consumer LLM product — layers, trade-offs, and the metric war between safety and usefulness.
points: Start with policy, not models: a written taxonomy of what's disallowed, by category and severity, with product-context nuance (medical questions ≠ medical advice ≠ self-harm content) — classifiers implement policy; they can't substitute for having one.

Pipeline layers: input screening (moderation classifier + injection/jailbreak heuristics before the model), the model's own trained refusals (necessary, insufficient — jailbreaks exist and always will), output screening (category classifiers, PII detection), and response shaping — for sensitive-but-legitimate queries, route to safe-completion styles rather than binary block/allow.

The metric war: false negatives (harm gets through) vs false positives (over-refusal — legitimate users blocked, product degraded, users route around you). Measure both: violation rate on red-team sets AND refusal rate on benign sets; tune per category severity — asymmetric costs justify asymmetric thresholds.

Operations: human review queues for edge cases feeding policy refinement, red-teaming as a continuous program (adversarial prompts evolve), incident response with category-level rollbacks (tighten one category without lobotomizing the product), and audit trails for regulators.
Say the architecture principle: safety is a system property — model refusals + classifiers + rate limits + UX + policy — no single layer is load-bearing alone.

links.label: Content moderation pipelines & policy enforcement
links.target: 05-LLM-Production/11-Hallucination, Safety & Guardrails/06-Content moderation pipelines & policy enforcement

questions.badge: Trending — moderation-pipeline design recurs in consumer-AI JDs (2025–26)
questions.oneLiner: Write the policy first, then layer input screening, trained refusals, output classification, and safe-completion routing — measuring over-refusal on benign traffic as seriously as violations on red-team sets, because a safety system that blocks legitimate users is failing at a different metric, not succeeding.

questions.text: 🗣️ (jbtiq_llm Q36 · S13 Cross-Cutting & Frontier) "RLAIF and Constitutional AI: what problem in the RLHF pipeline do they attack, and what's the catch?
points: The attacked bottleneck: human preference labels — expensive, slow, inconsistent across annotators, and unscalable to the volume preference optimization wants. RLAIF replaces the human preference judgment with an AI judge; label throughput becomes effectively unlimited.

Constitutional AI structures the judge: an explicit set of written principles (the constitution) guides AI self-critique and revision (generate → critique against principles → revise) plus AI preference labeling — making the alignment target inspectable and editable as text rather than implicit in thousands of human choices.
Why it works at all: models are better at judging outputs against criteria than at generating perfectly — the generate-critique gap is the exploitable asymmetry.

The catches: bias inheritance and amplification (the AI judge's blind spots become the trained policy's blind spots, now at scale), self-preference loops, and the constitution's coverage problem — principles conflict and underdetermine hard cases, so who writes the constitution becomes the governance question.

Production relevance beyond frontier labs: the same pattern powers synthetic preference data for domain fine-tunes and LLM-judged eval pipelines — the scalability/bias trade is one you'll run yourself, in miniature.
questions.badge: Evergreen
questions.oneLiner: They replace the human-label bottleneck with AI judgment — Constitutional AI making the target an editable text document via critique-and-revise — buying unlimited label throughput at the cost of inheriting and amplifying the judge's biases, which is why judge calibration stays a human job.

questions.text: 🗣️ (jbtiq_llm Q37 · S13 Cross-Cutting & Frontier) "Multimodal LLMs: how do images actually get into a language model, and what changes operationally when you ship vision?
points: Mechanism: a vision encoder (ViT-family) turns the image into patch embeddings; a projector/adapter maps them into the LLM's embedding space; the decoder then attends over image tokens and text tokens in one sequence. Trained by alignment stages (caption/pair data, then multimodal instruction tuning). Native early-fusion architectures exist, but encoder+projector remains the workhorse pattern.

Operational change #1 — token economics: an image becomes hundreds-to-thousands of tokens depending on resolution/tiling; resolution strategy is a cost dial (detail vs bill), and context fills fast with multi-image inputs.

Operational change #2 — new failure modes: visual hallucination (confidently describing what isn't there), OCR brittleness on dense documents, spatial-reasoning weakness, and charts/tables read plausibly-wrong — your eval suite needs visual golden sets, and "faithfulness" now means faithful to the pixels.

Operational change #3 — safety surface widens: injection via text embedded in images (screenshot attacks), NSFW/PII in uploads, provenance questions — input moderation must scan the image channel too.

Architecture note: for document-heavy products, compare VLM-reads-the-page against OCR/layout-parser-then-LLM — the boring pipeline still wins on dense structured documents often enough to prototype both.
questions.badge: Trending — multimodal serving questions rising across JDs (2025–26)
questions.oneLiner: A vision encoder patches the image into embeddings a projector maps into the LLM's token space — after which images are just expensive tokens, bringing resolution-based cost dials, visual hallucination and image-borne injection as the new operational realities.

questions.text: 🗣️ (jbtiq_llm Q39 · S13 Cross-Cutting & Frontier) "Memorization and PII: when does a model regurgitate training data, and what does that mean for training on customer data?
points: The predictor is repetition and distinctiveness: strings seen many times (or highly unique/high-entropy ones like keys and emails in repeated contexts) get memorized verbatim; larger models memorize more. Deduplication is the single most effective training-side mitigation — it attacks the repetition driver directly.

Extraction is practical, not theoretical: adversarial prompting can recover memorized sequences; membership-inference attacks can sometimes establish that a record was trained on — which converts training-set contents into a disclosure risk with regulatory weight (GDPR-class erasure requests are near-impossible to honor inside weights).

Policy consequences for customer data: default answer is don't train on raw customer data — scrub PII at ingestion, aggregate/synthesize, get explicit consent tiers; fine-tunes on tenant data must be per-tenant isolated (a shared model fine-tuned on everyone's tickets can leak tenant A's content to tenant B).

Inference-side controls: output PII detection/redaction as a guardrail layer, canary strings in sensitive corpora to detect memorization empirically, differential-privacy training where the math is worth the utility cost (rarely, but say it exists).
The governance sentence: weights are a data store you can't query, audit, or delete from — classify them accordingly, and let that framing drive what's allowed in.
