questions.text: 🗣️ (jbtiq_llm Q40 · S13 Cross-Cutting & Frontier) "Pick benchmarks for a model-selection decision: what does the public leaderboard tell you, and what's your private protocol?
points: Leaderboard limits: contamination (test sets leak into training — scores inflate unverifiably), saturation (top models cluster within noise on old benchmarks), and task mismatch (MMLU-style knowledge doesn't predict your extraction accuracy or refusal behavior). Arena-style human preference boards add preference-for-style bias (verbosity, formatting) — useful signal for chat, weak for task quality.

What public numbers are still good for: coarse capability tiering (is the model in the frontier class or not), trend direction across generations, and spotting specialized strengths (code vs math vs multilingual boards diverge).

The private protocol: build a held-secret eval set from your real traffic (golden answers + rubrics), spanning your quality dimensions (task accuracy, format compliance, refusals, latency, cost per task); run candidates blind, same prompts and params; report per-dimension results with CIs, not one average.
Guard your own set like a benchmark author: never in any prompt or fine-tune, rotate/refresh over time, and re-run on every model-version change (silent updates again).
The sentence that lands: public benchmarks shortlist, private evals decide — anyone choosing a production model off a leaderboard is outsourcing the decision to a contaminated average.
questions.badge: Trending — benchmark-skepticism questions recur in senior LLM screens (2025–26)
questions.oneLiner: Leaderboards suffer contamination, saturation, and task mismatch — use them to shortlist a tier, then decide with a held-secret eval from your own traffic, scored per dimension with confidence intervals, and re-run whenever the provider ships a new version.

questions.text: 🗣️ (jbtiq_llm Q41 · S13 Cross-Cutting & Frontier) "The residual stream: give me the mental model, and one practical thing it explains about model behavior.
points: The mental model: the transformer isn't a pipeline where each layer transforms the whole representation — there's a shared residual stream (the running vector at each position) that every attention head and MLP reads from and additively writes to. Layers are contributors to a common workspace, not sequential filters.

Consequences of additivity: information persists by default (a layer that writes nothing leaves the stream intact), features are superposed (more features than dimensions, packed non-orthogonally), and later layers can read early-layer writes directly — the stream is the model's working memory across depth.

One practical thing it explains: why interventions work — steering vectors (adding a direction to the stream changes behavior semantically), activation patching for causal attribution, and why probing at intermediate layers finds increasingly abstract features (early = syntax-ish, late = task/semantic).
It also grounds intuitions about depth: circuits are distributed across read-write patterns between heads, which is why single-layer explanations of behavior are usually wrong.
Keep the claim calibrated: this is the mechanistic-interpretability frame, productive but incomplete — superposition makes clean feature extraction genuinely hard (hence sparse autoencoder research).
questions.badge: Evergreen (interpretability-literacy check at senior level)
questions.oneLiner: Every head and MLP reads from and additively writes to one shared residual stream — the model's working memory across depth — which is why steering vectors work, why probes find increasingly abstract features by layer, and why features are superposed rather than neatly one-per-neuron.

questions.text: 🗣️ (jbtiq_llm Q42 · S13 Cross-Cutting & Frontier) "Training-run engineering: you're running a multi-week training job on hundreds of GPUs. What actually goes wrong, and what does the discipline look like?
points: Hardware attrition is routine at scale: with hundreds of GPUs over weeks, node failures are a when, not an if — so frequent checkpointing with fast distributed save/restore, automatic failure detection and job restart, and spare capacity are the baseline; time-to-recover multiplies into real money.

Loss-spike management: spikes and divergences happen (bad data batches, numeric instability at low precision, optimizer state issues) — the playbook is skip-the-batch, rewind-to-checkpoint with data-order change, gradient clipping, and careful LR/warmup schedules; bf16 exists because fp16's range made this worse.

Determinism and bookkeeping: exact data order logged (to replay around bad batches), every run's config/seed/commit recorded, and eval checkpoints on schedule — an unreproducible multi-week run is an unaccountable one.

Throughput engineering: MFU (model FLOPs utilization) as the honest efficiency metric; parallelism layout (data/tensor/pipeline) tuned to interconnect topology; stragglers and network flakes monitored — a few percent MFU is a large check at this scale.

Why it matters to an architect who'll never pretrain: the same disciplines — checkpointing, failure-resume, run bookkeeping, throughput accounting — apply to your fine-tuning and batch-inference jobs, scaled down.
questions.badge: Evergreen (tests whether "pretraining" knowledge is operational or theoretical)
questions.oneLiner: At multi-week multi-node scale, hardware failure and loss spikes are routine — so the discipline is fast checkpoint-resume, a spike playbook of rewind-and-skip, exact data-order bookkeeping for reproducibility, and MFU accounting, because a few lost percent is a large invoice.

questions.text: 🗣️ (jbtiq_llm Q43 · S13 Cross-Cutting & Frontier) "Beyond LoRA: what's in the wider PEFT toolbox, and when would you pick something other than LoRA?
points: The map: prompt/prefix tuning (learn soft tokens prepended to input/attention — tiny footprint, zero architecture change, historically weaker on hard tasks and small models), adapter layers (small bottleneck MLPs inserted per layer — the pre-LoRA classic, adds inference latency unless merged), IA3-style scaling (learn per-activation scaling vectors — even fewer parameters), and selective-layer/bias-only tuning (BitFit-class).
Why LoRA won the default slot: no inference overhead after merge, strong quality across scales, ecosystem/tooling gravity, and multi-adapter serving — the alternatives survive in niches.

When to pick differently: soft prompts when you can't touch weights at all (serving stack forbids adapters) or need thousands of ultra-cheap task variants; adapters/IA3 in research settings comparing parameter-efficiency frontiers; bias/selective tuning for tiny quick calibrations.
The decision variables are consistent: trainable-parameter budget, inference-latency tolerance, how many task variants must be served concurrently, and whether the base weights are modifiable at all.
Meta-point: PEFT choices are converging — the differentiator in practice is data quality and eval discipline, not which 0.5% of parameters you trained; say that before an interviewer says it to you.
questions.badge: Evergreen
questions.oneLiner: The toolbox trades where trainable parameters live — soft prompts in the input, adapters in the layers, IA3 in scalings — but LoRA's merge-to-zero-overhead and multi-adapter serving won the default, and in practice the fine-tune's quality is decided by data and evals, not by which PEFT you picked.

questions.text: 🗣️ (jbtiq_llm Q44 · S13 Cross-Cutting & Frontier) "Calibration and uncertainty: how do you get a trustworthy 'how sure is the model' signal out of an LLM system?
points: The baseline problem: pretrained models are decently calibrated at token level; post-training (RLHF/DPO) damages calibration — models become confident-sounding regardless of correctness, and verbalized certainty ("I'm 90% sure") correlates weakly with accuracy.

Signal families: logprob-based (token/sequence likelihood, entropy — cheap, available, needs recalibration per task via a small labeled set and temperature scaling / isotonic mapping); consistency-based (sample k answers, measure agreement — semantic entropy-style; expensive but the strongest practical signal for free-form answers, disagreement flags confabulation); verbalized confidence (ask the model — usable only after you've measured its reliability on your task, usually the weakest alone).
Combine and calibrate: whatever raw signal, map it to real probabilities against labeled outcomes (reliability curves again — same discipline as classical ML), per task, re-checked per model version.

What the number is for — the architecture part: selective prediction (answer / hedge / retrieve-more / escalate-to-human thresholds), routing (low confidence → bigger model or verification pass), and honest UX (show sources and hedge language below threshold).
The trap to name: don't ship raw logprobs or verbalized percentages to users or downstream logic — uncalibrated confidence is worse than none, because it transfers false trust.
questions.badge: Trending — uncertainty-quantification recurs in high-stakes-domain JDs (2025–26)
questions.oneLiner: Post-training wrecks native calibration, so build the signal — logprobs recalibrated on labeled outcomes, sampling agreement for free-form answers, verbalized confidence only after auditing it — and spend it on selective prediction: answer, verify, or escalate by threshold.

questions.text: 🗣️ (jbtiq_llm Q45 · S13 Cross-Cutting & Frontier) "Close it out: two model generations from now, which parts of your LLM architecture survive unchanged — and how does that shape what you build today?
points: Made obsolete by better models: elaborate prompt scaffolding, multi-step orchestration that compensates for reasoning gaps, some routing complexity, patch-the-model guardrail layers — engineering that substitutes for capability depreciates with every release.

Made more valuable: evals and golden sets (you can now measure the upgrade), retrieval infrastructure and data quality (a better reasoner over better context compounds), tool/API contracts (a stronger model exploits the same tools harder), traces and feedback loops. Engineering that feeds capability appreciates.
Untouched: identity/permissions/audit, cost governance, data pipelines and contracts, domain knowledge encoded in schemas and workflows — the classical-software substrate.

The design heuristic that follows: before building compensating machinery, ask "does this get deleted when the model improves?" — if yes, keep it thin and disposable; invest the durable dollars in evals, data, tools, and governance. Architect so a model swap is a config change plus an eval run.

End on the operating cadence: model upgrades are a scheduled institutional process — re-run gates, re-tune routing thresholds, re-check calibration, retire scaffolding — the orgs that win treat capability arrival as an intake pipeline, not a surprise.
questions.badge: Trending — the strategy synthesis senior LLM loops end on (2025–26)
questions.oneLiner: Scaffolding that substitutes for capability depreciates; evals, retrieval, tools and governance appreciate — so I keep compensating machinery thin, make model swap a config-plus-eval-run event, and run upgrades as a scheduled process, because the fastest-improving component in the stack is the one I don't build.

questions.text: 🗣️ (jbtiq_dl Q13 · S3 Transformer Architecture Core) "Why the √d_k in scaled dot-product attention — what actually breaks without it?
points: Dot products of d_k-dimensional vectors with unit-variance components have variance ≈ d_k — logit magnitude grows with head dimension.
Large-magnitude logits push softmax into saturation: output is nearly one-hot, and the softmax Jacobian ≈ 0 → tiny gradients, attention stops learning.
Dividing by √d_k renormalizes logit variance to ~1, keeping softmax in its sensitive, trainable regime.

Frame it as variance control — the same discipline as weight init and normalization, applied to attention logits. At long context the numerics of many/large logits resurface and kernels manage softmax stability explicitly.

questions.text: 🗣️ (jbtiq_dl Q14 · S3 Transformer Architecture Core) "Why multiple attention heads instead of one big head with the same total dimension?
points: One head = one softmax distribution per token — a single convex mixture; it must average all the relationships a token cares about into one set of weights.
H heads = H independent lookups in different learned subspaces — one can track syntax, another coreference, another positional patterns, simultaneously.
Each head is low-rank (d_model/H), so total compute stays roughly constant — you're spending the same budget on diversity instead of resolution.
Output = concat of heads through W_O, which learns to mix them.
Senior nuance: trained models show heavy head redundancy — many heads are prunable post-hoc — but training with multiplicity still helps optimization.
questions.badge: Evergreen
questions.oneLiner: One head gives each token a single attention distribution; multiple heads give several independent low-rank lookups in different subspaces for the same compute — different relationship types in parallel.

questions.text: 🗣️ (jbtiq_dl Q16 · S3 Transformer Architecture Core) "Pre-norm vs post-norm — and why LayerNorm instead of BatchNorm in transformers in the first place?
points: Post-norm (original 2017): normalize after the residual add → the residual path itself passes through norms; deep stacks become unstable and demand careful warmup.

Pre-norm: normalize inside the branch, residual path stays a pure identity highway → gradients reach every depth; the reason very deep LLMs train reliably. Standard today; post-norm's minor quality edge at small depth is the trade.
BatchNorm normalizes across the batch → depends on other examples: breaks with variable sequence lengths/padding, small microbatches, and creates train/inference statistics mismatch (running means).
LayerNorm normalizes across features per token — batch-independent, identical behavior train and serve. RMSNorm drops mean-centering for the same effect, cheaper — the current LLM default.
questions.badge: Trending — flagged in senior DL guides (Exponent, DataInterview) as the question that separates paper-readers from practitioners (2025–26)
questions.oneLiner: Pre-norm keeps the residual stream an untouched identity path, which is what makes very deep transformers trainable — and LayerNorm/RMSNorm normalize per token, so nothing depends on batch composition the way BatchNorm does.

questions.text: 🗣️ (jbtiq_dl Q17 · S3 Transformer Architecture Core) "Thought experiment: you delete every residual connection from a 24-layer transformer. What happens when you train it, and why?
points: It effectively doesn't train: every gradient must now pass through 24 stacks of attention/FFN/norms — you've reinstated the vanishing-signal problem residuals were built to kill.
Residuals give an identity path: the block computes a delta, x + f(x), so each layer refines a shared residual stream rather than wholesale re-encoding it.
Useful mental model: a residual network behaves like an ensemble of shallow paths — most gradient flows through short paths, deep paths are optional refinements.
Interplay: pre-norm keeps that path clean (Q16), and init schemes deliberately scale residual-branch outputs down so the network starts near the identity.
This "residual stream as shared workspace" view is also the load-bearing abstraction in interpretability work (Q45).

questions.badge: Evergreen
questions.oneLiner: Without residuals every layer must relearn the whole representation and gradients must survive 24 nonlinear blocks — with them, each block writes a small delta onto an identity highway, which is what makes depth trainable.

questions.text: 🗣️ (jbtiq_dl Q23 · S4 Modern Transformer Variants) "Your PM wants a million-token context window. What breaks first, and what are the architectural levers?
points: Decode memory breaks first: KV cache grows linearly with context (Q18) — at million-token scale it dwarfs the weights per request. Levers: GQA, KV quantization, paging, offload.
Prefill compute is O(n²): time-to-first-token becomes the user-facing pain; FlashAttention and chunked prefill manage it, but the quadratic is still there.
Positional generalization: RoPE beyond trained length degrades — needs scaling/extension schemes plus long-context finetuning; you can't just crank a config value.
Restricted attention patterns (sliding window locally, a few global tokens) cut cost to near-linear — trading exact global attention for reach.
The honest caveat: a window accepted ≠ a window used — retrieval quality across the middle of huge contexts must be evaluated, not assumed.
